Initial Data Quality Observations¶

The dataset contains 11,260 customer account records and 19 variables, including the target variable Churn.

Key observations:

  1. The overall churn rate is approximately 16.84%, indicating that churned accounts represent a minority of the dataset. This class imbalance will need to be considered during model development.
  2. Customer care interactions vary considerably across accounts, with some recording up to 132 contacts in the previous year.
  3. Average service satisfaction and customer care satisfaction scores are approximately 2.90 and 3.07, respectively.
  4. Several numerical variables have been incorrectly classified as categorical because they contain special characters such as #, @, $, +, and *.
  5. Missing values exist across multiple variables, with cashback, Complain_ly, and Day_Since_CC_connect having the highest initially observed missing percentages.
  6. No duplicate records or account identifiers were identified.

Conclusion: The dataset requires additional cleaning, particularly numerical type conversion, missing-value treatment, and categorical consistency checks, before reliable exploratory analysis can be performed.

Numerical Distribution Analysis - Key Observations¶

The numerical distribution analysis revealed the following:

  • Skewed variables: Monthly revenue, cashback, tenure, coupon usage, and days since customer care contact exhibit positive skewness.
  • Potential outliers: Extreme values were observed in monthly revenue (140), cashback (1,997), tenure (99), and customer care contacts (132). These require further investigation before treatment.
  • Account composition: Most accounts contain three or four users, indicating that account-level churn can affect multiple customers.
  • Customer satisfaction: Service satisfaction scores are concentrated around 2–4, while customer care satisfaction scores span 1-5.
  • Imputation considerations: Median imputation is a reasonable candidate for skewed numerical variables, while mode imputation may be appropriate for discrete account user counts.

Conclusion: The dataset contains skewed distributions and potentially influential observations. Outlier treatment should consider business relevance, particularly for revenue-generating accounts, rather than removing extreme values indiscriminately.

Investigate outliers before imputation¶

Investigating the unusual values in Tenure, rev_per_month, cashback and CC_Contacted_LY

# Investigate potentially extreme values
outlier_checks = {
    "Tenure": 90,
    "rev_per_month": 50,
    "cashback": 500,
    "CC_Contacted_LY": 60
}

outlier_results = []

for col, threshold in outlier_checks.items():
    extreme = df_clean[df_clean[col] > threshold]

    outlier_results.append({
        "Variable": col,
        "Threshold": threshold,
        "Accounts": len(extreme),
        "Percentage (%)": round(
            len(extreme) / len(df_clean) * 100, 2
        ),
        "Min Extreme": extreme[col].min(),
        "Max Extreme": extreme[col].max(),
        "Churn Rate (%)": round(
            extreme["Churn"].mean() * 100, 2
        ) if len(extreme) > 0 else 0
    })

outlier_summary = pd.DataFrame(outlier_results)

Outlier Investigation - Findings¶

An investigation of four potentially anomalous numerical variables identified 348 accounts (3.09% of the dataset) with extreme values.

The analysis revealed that none of these accounts had overlapping outlier flags. Each affected account exhibited an extreme value in only one of the investigated variables.

The unusual observations included tenure of 99, monthly revenue between 100 and 140, cashback between 1,800 and 1,997, and customer care contact counts between 126 and 132.

Although these observations are unusual, there is insufficient evidence to classify them definitively as errors. Consequently, they will be retained during exploratory analysis, with further investigation and sensitivity testing planned before predictive modeling.

Business implication: Removing extreme revenue observations without verification could exclude commercially valuable accounts and distort the development of targeted retention strategies.

Check whether missing values are associated with churn¶

Before imputing missing values, we need to determine whether missingness differs between churned and retained accounts. For example, if monthly revenue is missing more frequently among churned accounts, that missingness could itself carry predictive information.

In [19]:
# Analyze missingness by churn status
missing_by_churn = []

for col in df_clean.columns.drop(["AccountID", "Churn"]):
    missing_by_churn.append({
        "Variable": col,
        "Retained Missing (%)": round(
            df_clean[df_clean["Churn"] == 0][col].isna().mean() * 100, 2
        ),
        "Churned Missing (%)": round(
            df_clean[df_clean["Churn"] == 1][col].isna().mean() * 100, 2
        )
    })

missing_by_churn_df = pd.DataFrame(missing_by_churn)

missing_by_churn_df["Difference (pp)"] = (
    missing_by_churn_df["Churned Missing (%)"] - missing_by_churn_df["Retained Missing (%)"]
).round(2)

display(
    missing_by_churn_df.sort_values(

    )

Missing Value Treatment¶

Missing values were handled according to variable characteristics. Median imputation was applied to numerical variables because several distributions were skewed. Mode imputation was applied to account user counts, while missing categorical values were assigned an explicit Unknown category. These transformations create an analysis-ready dataset for exploratory data analysis.

In [20]:
# Preserve the converted dataset
df_eda = df_clean.copy()

# Numerical variables
numeric_features = [
    "Tenure",
    "Account_user_count",
    "rev_per_month",
    "rev_growth_yoy",
    "coupon_used_for_payment",
    "Day_Since_CC_connect",
    "cashback",
    "CC_Contacted_LY",
    "Service_Score",
    "CC_Agent_Score",
    "City_Tier",
    "Complain_ly"
]

# Impute numerical variables using the median
for col in numeric_features:
    if col == "Account_user_count":
        df_eda[col] = df_eda[col].fillna(
            df_eda[col].mode().iloc[0]
        )
    else:
        df_eda[col] = df_eda[col].fillna(
            df_eda[col].median()
        )

# Identify categorical variables
categorical_features = df_eda.select_dtypes(
    include=["object", "str", "category"]
).columns

# Replace missing categorical values
for col in categorical_features:
    df_eda[col] = df_eda[col].fillna("Unknown")

# Verify remaining missing values
print("Total missing values:", df_eda.isnull().sum().sum())

print("Dataset shape:", df_eda.shape)

Categorical Data Standardization¶

Categorical variables were examined for inconsistent labels and invalid values. Equivalent account segment labels were standardized, and invalid login device values were assigned to the Unknown category. Missing categorical values had previously been labeled Unknown to preserve the original account records.

Categorical Data Cleaning - Key Observations¶

Categorical data inspection identified inconsistent gender labels, account segment naming variations, and invalid login device values.

The following standardization rules were applied:

  • Gender categories M and F were standardized to Male and Female.
  • Account segment labels Regular + and Super + were standardized to Regular Plus and Super Plus.
  • Invalid login device entries represented by &&&& were reclassified as Unknown.
  • Existing valid payment and marital status categories were preserved.

These transformations improved categorical consistency without removing account records.

Conclusion: The cleaned dataset is suitable for exploratory analysis. Potential numerical outliers have been retained pending further investigation, and preprocessing decisions have been documented for reproducibility.

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

Target Variable Analysis¶

The objective of this analysis is to examine the distribution of the target variable (Churn) and determine the proportion of accounts that have churned.

Understanding the churn distribution is essential for assessing class imbalance and selecting appropriate model evaluation metrics during the model development phase.

In [26]:
# Calculate churn distribution
churn_counts = df_eda["Churn"].value_counts().sort_index()

churn_percentages = (
    df_eda["Churn"].value_counts(normalize=True)
    .sort_index() * 100
)

churn_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Account Count": churn_counts,
    "Percentage (%)": churn_percentages.round(2)
})

churn_summary.index = ["Retained", "Churned"]

Key Observations and Business Insights¶

  1. Overall churn rate: Approximately 16.84% of customer accounts have churned, while 83.16% remain active.

  2. Class imbalance: The dataset contains substantially more retained accounts than churned accounts, resulting in a moderately imbalanced target distribution.

  3. Business significance: Approximately one in six accounts has churned. Because a single account may represent multiple customers, the business impact could extend beyond the number of accounts lost.

  4. Modeling implications: A model that predicts every account as retained would achieve approximately 83.16% accuracy but would fail to identify any churned accounts. Therefore, accuracy alone will not be sufficient to evaluate model performance. Recall, precision, F1-score, and precision-recall AUC will be considered during model development.

  5. Retention opportunity: The churn distribution establishes a baseline for investigating which customer segments are more likely to churn and where targeted retention campaigns may be most valuable.

Conclusion: Customer churn represents a meaningful business challenge. The analysis supports developing a predictive solution that identifies at-risk accounts while accounting for class imbalance and the financial costs of retention interventions.

Univariate Numerical Analysis¶

Univariate analysis examines each numerical variable independently to understand its distribution, central tendency, variability, and potential outliers.

This analysis focuses on customer tenure, account size, monthly revenue, revenue growth, customer satisfaction, customer care interactions, coupon usage, and cashback.

The objective is to establish customer account characteristics that may be relevant to churn prediction and retention campaign design.

Univariate Numerical Analysis — Observations and Business Implications¶

Key observations

  1. Revenue distribution: Monthly revenue is highly right-skewed (skewness = 9.44), indicating that most accounts generate relatively low revenue while a small number have unusually high recorded values.

  2. Cashback distribution: Cashback is also highly right-skewed (skewness = 8.97). The wide variation suggests differences in cashback amounts across customer accounts.

  3. Account tenure: Tenure exhibits substantial positive skewness (3.94), with a median of 9. This indicates that many accounts have relatively short tenure, while a smaller proportion have much longer recorded tenure.

  4. Customer care interactions: The median number of customer care contacts is 16, with some accounts recording exceptionally high contact frequencies.

  5. Service satisfaction: Service satisfaction is concentrated around a score of 3, with an average of 2.90.

  6. Customer care satisfaction: Customer care ratings are more widely distributed, with an average of 3.07.

Business implications

  • Revenue variation highlights the importance of considering account value when designing retention campaigns.
  • Differences in tenure may justify investigating whether newer and established accounts exhibit different churn patterns.
  • Customer satisfaction and customer care engagement are promising dimensions for churn analysis.
  • Extreme observations should be investigated rather than automatically removed, as some may represent commercially important accounts.

Conclusion

The analysis demonstrates considerable variation in account characteristics and customer experiences. These findings provide a foundation for bivariate analysis to determine which variables are associated with customer churn.

Univariate Categorical Analysis - Key Findings¶

The categorical analysis reveals the following customer account characteristics:

  1. Account segmentation: Regular Plus (36.63%) and Super (36.07%) are the dominant account segments, collectively representing 72.70% of the customer base.

  2. Payment preferences: Debit Card (40.74%) and Credit Card (31.18%) are the most common payment methods, together accounting for 71.92% of accounts.

  3. Gender distribution: Male primary account holders represent 59.54% of accounts, compared with 39.50% female account holders.

  4. Marital status: Married primary account holders represent 52.04% of the customer base, followed by single (31.26%) and divorced (14.81%) customers.

  5. Login device: Mobile is the most frequently used login device (66.45%), followed by computers (26.80%).

  6. City tier: Tier 1 cities account for 65.50% of customer accounts, followed by Tier 3 (30.24%) and Tier 2 (4.26%).

Business implications

The concentration of accounts in Regular Plus and Super segments suggests that these groups may be important for retention planning. The prevalence of card payments and mobile access also provides useful context for designing customer engagement campaigns.

However, account volume alone does not establish churn risk. Further analysis is required to determine which categories exhibit disproportionately high churn rates.

Conclusion

The customer base is concentrated in specific account segments, payment methods, device preferences, and geographic tiers. These characteristics provide a foundation for investigating churn patterns across customer groups.

Bivariate Analysis - Numerical Variables vs. Churn¶

Bivariate analysis examines the relationship between individual customer characteristics and account churn.

The objective is to identify numerical variables associated with churn and understand how churned accounts differ from retained accounts.

These findings will help identify potential churn predictors and inform subsequent retention campaign recommendations.

Bivariate Numerical Analysis — Key Findings¶

The comparison of numerical variables across churned and retained accounts revealed several notable patterns.

  1. Account tenure: Churned accounts have a median tenure of 1, compared with 10 for retained accounts. This substantial difference suggests that shorter-tenure accounts may be more vulnerable to churn.

  2. Cashback: Churned accounts have a lower median cashback value (153.46) than retained accounts (166.15). Further analysis is required to determine whether cashback is meaningfully associated with retention.

  3. Customer care interactions: Churned accounts have a slightly higher median number of customer care contacts (17) compared with retained accounts (16).

  4. Monthly revenue: Both groups have the same median monthly revenue of 5, suggesting that revenue alone may not clearly distinguish churned from retained accounts at the median.

  5. Customer satisfaction: Service satisfaction and customer care satisfaction have identical medians across both groups. However, their distributions may differ, warranting further investigation.

Business implications

  • Short-tenure accounts represent a promising segment for investigating early retention interventions.
  • Customer care interaction frequency may help identify accounts experiencing service-related difficulties.
  • Cashback and financial incentives should be evaluated carefully to ensure that retention benefits justify campaign costs.

Conclusion

Tenure demonstrates the clearest difference between churned and retained accounts in the current numerical analysis. Cashback and customer care interactions also show potentially useful patterns. These findings are observational and require further validation before being translated into retention campaign recommendations.

Bivariate Categorical Analysis - Key Findings¶

The analysis identified meaningful differences in churn rates across customer categories.

Key findings

  1. Account segment: Regular Plus has the highest churn rate among known segments (27.33%) and contributes approximately 59.4% of all churned accounts. This makes it a priority for further investigation.

  2. Payment method: Cash on Delivery (25.05%) and E wallet (22.68%) have higher churn rates than card-based payment methods.

  3. Marital status: Single account holders exhibit a churn rate of 26.90%, substantially higher than married account holders (11.48%).

  4. Login device: Computer users have a churn rate of 19.78%, compared with 15.66% among mobile users.

  5. City tier: Tier 3 accounts have the highest churn rate (21.35%), followed by Tier 2 (20.00%) and Tier 1 (14.55%).

  6. Gender: Male account holders have a slightly higher churn rate (17.68%) than female account holders (15.49%).

Business implications

Regular Plus represents a promising retention opportunity because of its combination of elevated churn risk and substantial account volume.

Payment methods and geographic segments also show differences worth investigating.

However, these findings are descriptive associations and should not be interpreted as causal relationships.

Conclusion

Account segment is a particularly important dimension for further churn investigation. Combining segment-level churn analysis with tenure, account revenue, and customer experience may help identify actionable retention opportunities.

Correlation Analysis¶

This section investigates the relationships between numerical customer attributes and churn using Spearman correlation.

Spearman correlation is selected because several numerical variables are skewed and contain extreme observations.

Correlation Analysis - Key Findings¶

Spearman correlation was used to examine the monotonic relationships between numerical customer characteristics and churn.

Key findings

  1. Tenure: Account tenure has the strongest observed correlation with churn (ρ = −0.401). Longer-tenure accounts tend to have lower churn.

  2. Customer care recency: Days since the last customer care contact has a weak negative correlation with churn (ρ = −0.171), suggesting that more recent customer care interactions may be associated with churn.

  3. Cashback: Cashback has a weak negative correlation with churn (ρ = −0.161). However, cashback is positively correlated with tenure (ρ = +0.42), indicating a potential confounding relationship.

  4. Customer care satisfaction: Customer care satisfaction has a weak positive correlation with churn (ρ = +0.104), warranting further investigation.

  5. Revenue and service satisfaction: Monthly revenue (ρ = +0.034) and service satisfaction (ρ = +0.006) show negligible monotonic relationships with churn.

Business implications

Tenure emerges as a promising variable for identifying accounts potentially vulnerable to churn.

Customer care engagement and cashback may provide additional predictive information, but their relationships should be evaluated alongside tenure and other account characteristics.

Conclusion

The correlation analysis identifies tenure as the strongest numerical association with churn. However, correlation does not imply causation, and weak correlations do not necessarily mean that a variable has no predictive value. Further segmentation and multivariate modeling are required.

Tenure-Based Churn Analysis¶

This analysis investigates how churn varies across different account tenure groups.

The objective is to identify periods in the customer lifecycle associated with elevated churn and determine whether early-life accounts represent a priority for retention interventions.

The analysis also examines how tenure interacts with account segmentation.

In [39]:
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# Create a copy for tenure analysis
tenure_df = df_eda.copy()

# Define tenure bands
tenure_bins = [-1, 1, 3, 6, 12, 24, 36, float("inf")]

tenure_labels = [
    "0–1",
    "2–3",
    "4–6",
    "7–12",
    "13–24",
    "25–36",
    "37+"
]

tenure_df["Tenure_Group"] = pd.cut(
    tenure_df["Tenure"],
    bins=tenure_bins,
    labels=tenure_labels
)

# Calculate churn statistics by tenure group
tenure_churn = (
    tenure_df.groupby(
        "Tenure_Group",
        observed=True
    )["Churn"]
    .agg(
        Accounts="count",
        Churned="sum",
        Churn_Rate="mean"
    )
    .reset_index()
)

tenure_churn["Churn Rate (%)"] = (
    tenure_churn["Churn_Rate"] * 100
).round(2)

display(
    tenure_churn[
        ["Tenure_Group", "Accounts", "Churned", "Churn Rate (%)"]
    ]
)

Tenure-Based Churn Analysis - Key Findings¶

The analysis reveals a strong association between account tenure and churn.

Key findings

  1. Accounts with tenure of 0–1 have a churn rate of 51.9%, compared with the overall churn rate of 16.84%.

  2. Churn rates decline substantially in subsequent tenure groups, reaching 9.8% for tenure 2–3 and 6.2% for tenure 13–24.

  3. HNI accounts with tenure 0–1 exhibit the highest observed segment-level churn rate at 77.91% (127 of 163 accounts).

  4. Regular Plus accounts with tenure 0–1 have a churn rate of 53.10%, representing 917 churned accounts. This subgroup alone contributes approximately 48.4% of all churned accounts.

  5. Super accounts with tenure 0–1 have a churn rate of 42.77%, indicating that elevated early-tenure churn is present across multiple account segments.

  6. The 37+ tenure group exhibits an elevated churn rate of 17.3%. Previously identified extreme tenure values warrant additional validation before interpreting this group.

Business implications

Early-tenure accounts represent a promising focus for retention planning.

Regular Plus accounts warrant particular attention because they combine elevated churn rates with substantial churn volume.

HNI accounts may also deserve priority if their revenue contribution and potential retention value justify targeted interventions.

Conclusion

The analysis suggests that early account tenure is a key dimension for churn risk identification. Further investigation should examine revenue exposure, customer care experiences, and the potential economics of targeted retention campaigns before recommending specific offers.

Revenue Exposure Analysis¶

This analysis estimates the monthly revenue associated with churned accounts across customer segments and tenure groups.

The objective is to identify segments combining high churn risk, substantial account volume, and meaningful revenue exposure.

These estimates will support the development of financially informed retention campaign recommendations.

Revenue Exposure Analysis - Key Findings¶

The revenue exposure analysis identifies customer segments where observed churn is associated with substantial historical monthly revenue.

Key findings

  1. Regular Plus accounts with tenure 0–1 represent the largest observed exposure group, with 917 churned accounts and associated monthly revenue of 5,874 units.

  2. Super accounts with tenure 0–1 represent the second-largest exposure group, with 281 churned accounts and monthly revenue exposure of 1,914 units.

  3. HNI accounts with tenure 0–1 exhibit the highest churn rate (77.91%), with monthly revenue exposure of 907 units.

  4. Early-tenure accounts dominate the highest-ranked revenue exposure groups, reinforcing the importance of account tenure in churn analysis.

Business implications

The results suggest that targeted early-lifecycle retention initiatives may offer greater business value than broad, untargeted campaigns.

Regular Plus accounts represent a promising initial focus because they combine substantial churn volume and revenue exposure.

However, financial incentives should not be recommended without evaluating campaign costs, expected incremental retention, and contribution margins.

Conclusion

The analysis establishes a preliminary prioritization of customer segments based on churn risk, churn volume, and historical revenue exposure. These findings will inform the subsequent predictive modeling and campaign evaluation phases.

Final Data Quality Assessment and EDA Conclusions¶

Extreme value assessment

The dataset contains 105 accounts (0.93%) with monthly revenue exceeding 50. These accounts collectively represent 12,643 units of historical average monthly revenue and exhibit a churn rate of 21.90%.

Additionally, 131 accounts have a tenure value of 99, with an observed churn rate of 18.32%.

These extreme observations have been retained pending further validation because automatic removal could exclude potentially important accounts or distort the business analysis.

Key EDA conclusions

  1. Overall churn: 16.84% of the 11,260 accounts have churned.

  2. Tenure: Tenure is the strongest numerical variable associated with churn (Spearman ρ = −0.401). Accounts with tenure 0–1 have a churn rate of approximately 51.9%.

  3. Account segment: Regular Plus accounts exhibit a churn rate of 27.33% and contribute approximately 59.4% of all churned accounts.

  4. High-risk segment: Regular Plus accounts with tenure 0–1 represent 917 churned accounts, approximately 48.4% of all observed churn.

  5. Revenue exposure: Regular Plus accounts with tenure 0–1 have the highest observed historical monthly revenue exposure among the analyzed segment-tenure groups, at 5,874 units.

  6. Payment methods: Cash on Delivery and E wallet accounts have elevated churn rates of 25.05% and 22.68%, respectively.

  7. Customer care: Customer care engagement and satisfaction exhibit relatively weak associations with churn and require further investigation.

  8. Data quality: Missing values, inconsistent categorical labels, incorrectly classified numerical variables, and extreme observations were identified during preprocessing. Missing values have been handled, while extreme observations require further validation.

Overall conclusion

The exploratory analysis identifies early-tenure accounts, particularly those in the Regular Plus segment, as a promising focus for further churn prediction and retention planning.

These findings are descriptive and do not establish causation or the effectiveness of proposed interventions. Predictive modeling and financial evaluation are required before implementing targeted retention campaigns.

Executive Business Insights from EDA¶

Executive Summary¶

Exploratory analysis of 11,260 customer accounts identified an overall churn rate of 16.84%, representing 1,896 churned accounts.

The findings indicate that churn is not uniformly distributed across the customer base. Account tenure and customer segmentation show particularly notable differences in churn outcomes.

Five key findings emerged:

1. Early-tenure accounts face substantially elevated churn risk.

Accounts with tenure of 0–1 recorded a churn rate of 51.9%, approximately three times the overall rate. This suggests that early customer engagement and onboarding should be investigated as potential retention opportunities.

2. Regular Plus accounts contribute disproportionately to observed churn.

The Regular Plus segment recorded 1,127 churned accounts, representing approximately 59.4% of all churned accounts. Its churn rate of 27.33% is significantly higher in absolute terms than the overall observed rate of 16.84%.

3. Payment methods show meaningful differences in observed churn.

Cash on Delivery (25.05%) and E-wallet (22.68%) accounts recorded higher churn rates than Credit Card (14.21%) and Debit Card (15.30%) accounts. Further investigation is required to determine whether payment experience or other customer characteristics explain these differences.

4. Customer-care engagement is associated with churn, although the relationship is relatively weak.

Churned accounts recorded a slightly higher median number of customer-care contacts than retained accounts (17 versus 16). Additional analysis is required to understand whether repeated contacts reflect unresolved service issues.

5. Financial exposure should influence retention priorities.

Churn is concentrated in certain account segments and tenure groups. Retention interventions should therefore consider both churn probability and account-level financial value rather than applying uniform incentives across the customer base.

Preliminary Business Recommendations¶

Based on these findings, the following actions are proposed for further validation:

  • Improve early-tenure engagement: Investigate onboarding journeys and evaluate proactive customer engagement during the earliest stages of account tenure.
  • Prioritize Regular Plus accounts: Assess the underlying drivers of churn within the segment and identify opportunities for targeted retention.
  • Investigate payment-related friction: Examine whether payment reliability, convenience, or transaction experience contributes to differences in churn.
  • Strengthen service recovery analysis: Investigate repeated customer-care contacts and unresolved complaints as possible early warning signals.
  • Adopt value-based retention targeting: Use predicted churn probabilities, account value, and intervention costs to evaluate campaign profitability.

Implications for Predictive Modeling¶

The EDA findings suggest that account tenure, account segment, payment method, and customer-care engagement should be evaluated as potential predictors of churn.

However, observed statistical associations do not establish causal relationships.

The model-building phase will evaluate these variables jointly, identify predictive interactions, and determine their contribution to out-of-sample model performance.

Executive Conclusion¶

Customer churn is concentrated in identifiable groups, particularly early-tenure and Regular Plus accounts.

These findings provide an initial basis for prioritizing further investigation and designing targeted retention strategies.

The next phase will develop predictive models and evaluate financially sustainable retention opportunities, with the objective of improving customer retention without introducing unnecessary campaign expenditure.

Proposed Model-Building Methodology¶

Modeling Objective¶

The objective is to develop a supervised machine learning classification model that predicts the likelihood of customer account churn.

The target variable is Churn, where:

  • 0: Account retained
  • 1: Account churned

The model will estimate churn probabilities for individual accounts, enabling the business to identify at-risk accounts and prioritize retention campaigns.

The analysis will also support the identification of important churn-related factors and the development of financially sustainable retention strategies.

Data Preparation¶

The dataset consists of 11,260 customer accounts and 19 variables, including the target variable.

The following preprocessing steps are proposed:

  1. Feature selection: Exclude AccountID because it is a unique identifier rather than a meaningful predictive feature.
  2. Missing values: Apply appropriate imputation techniques for numerical and categorical variables. Imputation will be fitted using training data only.
  3. Categorical encoding: Apply One-Hot Encoding to nominal categorical variables such as Payment, Gender, account_segment, Marital_Status, and Login_device.
  4. Numerical transformations: Apply scaling where required, particularly for Logistic Regression.
  5. Outlier treatment: Retain potentially legitimate extreme observations while investigating unusual values such as tenure 99 and extreme monthly revenue. Evaluate the sensitivity of model performance to these observations.
  6. Feature engineering: Evaluate additional features such as tenure groups, customer-care contact frequency, and cashback-to-revenue ratio where appropriate.

Preprocessing operations will be implemented using scikit-learn pipelines to ensure consistency and prevent data leakage.

Training and Testing Strategy¶

The dataset will be divided into:

  • 80% training data
  • 20% testing data

Stratified sampling will preserve the proportion of churned and retained accounts in both datasets.

The training dataset will be used for model fitting, cross-validation, and hyperparameter tuning.

The testing dataset will remain untouched until final model evaluation.

Stratified 5-fold cross-validation will be used during model development.

Handling Class Imbalance¶

Exploratory analysis identified the following class distribution:

  • Retained accounts: 83.16%
  • Churned accounts: 16.84%

This indicates moderate class imbalance.

The following approaches will be considered:

  • Class weighting to increase the importance of churned accounts during training.
  • Evaluation using recall, precision, F1-score, and Precision-Recall AUC rather than accuracy alone.
  • Threshold optimization based on business objectives and retention campaign costs.
  • SMOTE, if required, applied only within training folds to prevent data leakage.

Candidate Machine Learning Models¶

Four classification algorithms are proposed.

1. Logistic Regression — Baseline Model

Provides an interpretable baseline for estimating churn probabilities and understanding relationships between customer attributes and churn.

2. Decision Tree Classifier

Captures nonlinear relationships and produces interpretable decision rules that may help explain churn behavior.

3. Random Forest Classifier

Combines multiple decision trees to improve predictive stability and capture complex feature interactions.

4. XGBoost Classifier

Uses gradient boosting to learn complex relationships and may improve predictive performance on structured customer data.

The models will be compared using consistent cross-validation procedures.

Model Evaluation¶

Model performance will be assessed using:

Metric Purpose
Recall Measures the proportion of actual churners correctly identified
Precision Measures the proportion of predicted churners who actually churn
F1-score Balances precision and recall
ROC-AUC Evaluates discrimination across classification thresholds
PR-AUC Evaluates performance on the minority churn class
Confusion Matrix Identifies false positives and false negatives

Primary evaluation focus: Recall and Precision-Recall AUC, with precision and campaign economics used to assess practical suitability.

The final classification threshold will be selected using validation data rather than automatically assuming a threshold of 0.5.

Model Interpretability¶

Model interpretability will be incorporated to explain the factors influencing churn predictions.

Techniques will include:

  • Logistic Regression coefficients.
  • Permutation feature importance.
  • SHAP analysis for suitable tree-based models.

Particular attention will be given to features identified during EDA, including tenure, account segment, payment method, and customer-care interactions.

Business-Oriented Model Evaluation¶

The ultimate objective is not simply to predict churn accurately but to support profitable customer retention.

Predicted churn probabilities will be combined with account revenue information to prioritize potential retention opportunities.

Proposed campaign evaluation will consider:

  • Predicted churn probability.
  • Expected account value or contribution margin.
  • Estimated effectiveness of retention interventions.
  • Campaign and incentive costs.
  • Expected incremental financial benefit.

A proposed decision framework is:

Expected Net Benefit = Expected Incremental Revenue Protected − Campaign Cost

Campaigns will be recommended only where the expected incremental financial benefit is positive.

Because churn prediction alone does not establish whether an intervention will prevent churn, campaign effectiveness will ideally be measured using controlled experiments.

Expected Outcome¶

The model-building phase is expected to deliver:

  1. A validated churn prediction model capable of estimating account-level churn probabilities.
  2. An understanding of the most important predictive factors.
  3. A prioritized list of accounts for potential retention interventions.
  4. A financially defensible framework for evaluating retention campaigns.

These outputs will support data-driven customer retention decisions while minimizing unnecessary campaign expenditure.

Project Action Plan¶

Overview¶

Milestone 1 established an understanding of customer account churn through data quality assessment, preprocessing, exploratory data analysis, and the identification of potential churn indicators.

The analysis covered 11,260 customer accounts, of which 1,896 (16.84%) had churned.

The next phase will focus on developing, evaluating, and interpreting predictive models that can identify accounts at risk of churn and support targeted, financially sustainable retention strategies.

Proposed Implementation Plan¶

Phase Activities Expected Deliverable
1. Data Preparation Finalize feature selection, preprocessing pipelines, categorical encoding, and stratified data splitting Model-ready training and testing datasets
2. Baseline Modeling Train Logistic Regression and Decision Tree classifiers Baseline model performance
3. Advanced Modeling Train Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers Comparative model results
4. Model Optimization Apply stratified cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning, and class imbalance handling Optimized candidate models
5. Model Evaluation Compare recall, precision, F1-score, ROC-AUC, and PR-AUC; assess probability calibration and classification thresholds Selected and validated churn prediction model
6. Model Interpretation Analyze feature importance and explain model predictions using appropriate interpretability techniques Key predictive churn factors
7. Campaign Strategy Combine churn probabilities with account value, intervention costs, and assumed campaign effectiveness Proposed targeted retention campaigns
8. Business Recommendations Evaluate expected campaign economics and recommend financially sustainable interventions Final business recommendations

Business Priorities Identified from EDA¶

The exploratory analysis identified several areas that warrant further investigation during model development.

Priority 1: Early-tenure accounts

Accounts with tenure between 0 and 1 recorded a churn rate of approximately 51.9%, compared with the overall churn rate of 16.84%.

This suggests that early customer engagement and onboarding should be investigated as potential retention opportunities.

Priority 2: Regular Plus accounts

Regular Plus accounts recorded a churn rate of 27.33%, with 1,127 churned accounts.

The segment represents a substantial concentration of churn and should receive particular attention during model development and campaign evaluation.

Priority 3: Customer-care engagement

Churned accounts had a slightly higher median number of customer-care contacts than retained accounts.

Customer-care interactions should therefore be evaluated as potential predictive indicators, although the observed association does not establish causation.

Priority 4: Revenue-sensitive retention

Account revenue and cashback distributions contain extreme values. Retention strategies should therefore consider account-level financial exposure rather than applying uniform incentives across all customers.

Proposed Retention Campaign Framework¶

The final model will assign churn probabilities to customer accounts.

These probabilities will be combined with financial information to prioritize accounts for potential retention interventions.

Possible interventions include:

  • Early-tenure onboarding: Proactive support and engagement for recently acquired accounts with elevated predicted churn risk.
  • Service recovery: Targeted customer-care follow-up for accounts exhibiting potential service-related dissatisfaction.
  • Segment-specific engagement: Personalized retention initiatives for high-risk customer segments.
  • Value-based incentives: Carefully controlled incentives for accounts where expected incremental retention benefits exceed intervention costs.

Campaign recommendations will be evaluated using estimated contribution margins, intervention effectiveness, and associated costs.

Where possible, controlled experiments will be proposed to measure whether campaigns actually reduce churn.

Success Criteria¶

The project will be evaluated against both technical and business objectives.

Technical success

  • Develop a model that improves on baseline churn prediction performance.
  • Demonstrate useful identification of churned accounts through recall and precision.
  • Evaluate generalization using cross-validation and an independent test dataset.
  • Provide interpretable predictions and identify important churn-related features.

Business success

  • Identify actionable customer segments with elevated churn risk.
  • Prioritize accounts according to churn probability and financial value.
  • Develop targeted campaign recommendations with measurable financial assumptions.
  • Establish a framework for assessing campaign profitability before implementation.

Expected Business Impact¶

The proposed solution is expected to support a shift from broad, reactive retention efforts toward targeted, data-driven customer engagement.

By identifying high-risk accounts and evaluating the financial implications of proposed interventions, the business can prioritize retention resources more effectively.

The final recommendations will focus on reducing avoidable account churn while protecting profitability.

Conclusion¶

Milestone 1 has established the analytical foundation for customer churn prediction.

The findings indicate that churn is not uniformly distributed across customer accounts, with particularly notable differences across tenure groups and account segments.

The next milestone will validate these relationships through predictive modeling and translate the results into financially defensible customer retention recommendations.
